title: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree
goal: By the end you can draw the job tree for a piece of coroutine code, predict what a failure or a cancel does to it, spot leaked work, and give a class that starts background work a scope it owns and closes.
opening:
A big dinner has a shape. The dinner has courses, and each course has dishes. The rule in every kitchen is simple: a course goes out only when all of its dishes are ready, and the dinner isn't over until every course has gone out.

Now the roast burns. The main course is off, so the cook takes the potatoes and the gravy off the heat too, and tells the family what happened. And if the guests phone to call the dinner off, everything comes off the stove: every course, every pan.

Coroutines follow the same rule, and it has a name, structured concurrency. The trap is stepping outside it without noticing, with one line that starts work nobody will ever wait for, like a pan left on in the neighbour's kitchen. In Builders, `coroutineScope` waited for its children and cancelled the rest when one failed. In this lesson, we'll draw the tree behind that, watch a failure travel up it and a cancel travel down, catch a leak, and give a class a scope it owns. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A dinner coroutine calls `GlobalScope.launch { simmerStock() }`. Then the guests call the dinner off, so the dinner coroutine is cancelled. What happens to the stock?
options: It's cancelled too, because the dinner started it
It keeps simmering: it belongs to GlobalScope, not to the dinner
It pauses until the dinner starts again
The JVM throws `IllegalStateException` when the dinner is cancelled
warmup.why: A cancel travels down a tree of parent and child jobs. `GlobalScope` has no job, so a coroutine launched there has no parent. Cancelling the dinner doesn't reach it, nobody waits for it, and nobody hears about its failure. It's a pan left on in the neighbour's kitchen.

sections.h: Every coroutine has a parent, and a parent waits for its children
sections.body:
Every coroutine you start with `launch` or `async` gets a **job**, a handle to its life that you can wait for or cancel. That job becomes a **child** of the job in the scope you started it in, and children can have children of their own. The result is a tree, and the tree is the whole idea behind **structured concurrency**: work that runs at the same time has the same nested shape as the code that started it.

Here's the dinner as code, with a name on every coroutine:

```kotlin
runBlocking(CoroutineName("dinner")) {                 // the root
    launch(CoroutineName("main-course")) {              // a child of dinner
        coroutineScope {                                // a node of its own
            async(CoroutineName("roast")) { /* ... */ }
            async(CoroutineName("potatoes")) { /* ... */ }
            launch(CoroutineName("gravy")) { /* ... */ }
        }
    }
}
```

```java
// Java equivalent: StructuredTaskScope (preview in JDK 25, JEP 505; needs --enable-preview)
try (var mainCourse = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {    // a node, like coroutineScope
    mainCourse.fork(() -> roast());
    mainCourse.fork(() -> potatoes());
    mainCourse.fork(() -> gravy());
    mainCourse.join();                                  // waits for all three subtasks
}
```

A **scope** is a coroutine context that holds a job. The **context** is the small set of settings that travels with a coroutine: its job, its name, its dispatcher (lesson 4 of this track takes it apart). `launch` reads the job from the scope's context and hangs the new coroutine under it. `coroutineScope` adds a node of its own, between its caller and the children started inside it.

The first rule of the tree is the kitchen's rule: **a parent can't complete until all of its children have completed.** When a coroutine's body ends, its job waits in a state called "completing" until every child is done. That's why `coroutineScope` returns only after its slowest child, and why `runBlocking` doesn't return while anything below it still runs. Finished children leave the tree, so `job.children` lists only the work still going.

`JobTree`, in the Try it below, prints the tree at 100 ms, while the three dishes are still cooking. Sketch the tree you expect first, then compare:

```text
tree at 100 ms, seen from the dinner coroutine:
dinner  active=true  children=1
    main-course  active=true  children=1
        main-course  active=true  children=3
            roast  active=true  children=0
            potatoes  active=true  children=0
            gravy  active=true  children=0
after join: dinner has 0 children
```

`main-course` shows up twice. The second one is the `coroutineScope`, a node of its own, which copies its parent's context, name included. Under it sit the three dishes. After `join`, the dinner has no children left, because finished children leave the tree.

The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 docs spell out four rules for how lives in the tree affect each other. A parent waits for its children. Cancelling a parent cancels its children. A child that fails with an exception cancels its parent, unless the parent is a supervisor (lesson 6 of this track). And a child that ends with `CancellationException`, the exception a cancelled coroutine throws, counts as cancelled, not failed, so the parent isn't told.

The middle two rules are where the kitchen gets busy.

sections.h: Failure goes up, cancellation goes down
sections.body:
Take the main course from the last section: roast, potatoes and gravy, three children of one `coroutineScope`. At 100 ms the roast burns and throws `BurnedException`, an exception the demo defines for a ruined dish. Here's what the tree does, in order:

1. The roast child fails. It reports the exception to its parent, the scope.
2. The scope's job is cancelled with that exception. A cancelled job cancels all of its children, so the potatoes and the gravy are cancelled, and their `finally` blocks run.
3. The scope waits until those children have really stopped.
4. `coroutineScope` rethrows the `BurnedException` to its caller, which can catch it like any exception.

So one failure takes down the whole subtree it belongs to, then comes out as one exception at the place that started the work. The total time is the time to the failure, about 100 ms, not the time of the slowest dish. Nothing is left running in the background.

`FailureSpreads`, in the Try it below, does this with two children: a roast that burns at 100 ms, and potatoes that would take a second. Predict which lines print, and when. On this busy machine it printed:

```text
[   6 ms] scope body finished; the scope now waits for its children
[ 161 ms] roast: burned, throwing BurnedException
[ 163 ms] potatoes: finally block runs
[ 165 ms] caller caught: the roast burned
```

`potatoes: done` never printed. Two milliseconds after the roast burned, the potatoes were off the heat, and two more later the caller had the exception. (The first `delay` read 161 ms instead of 100 because a JVM, the program that runs the code, is slow just after it starts. That part is the machine, not the tree.)

The Java twin is the honest contrast. An executor, Java's pool that runs submitted tasks, has no tree, so after the roast fails, the potatoes carry on to `potatoes: done` at about 1,000 ms, and `close()` waits for them. To stop them, you cancel them by hand, which is the step `coroutineScope` does for you.

Cancellation only travels **down**. If the caller cancels the dinner, because the guests called it off or a timeout fired, every coroutine below it is cancelled. A child that's cancelled doesn't cancel its parent. A child whose block ends by throwing `CancellationException` is treated the same way: "cancelled", not "failed", and the parent carries on.

**A failure goes up the tree and stops the siblings. A cancel goes down and stops there.**

This is the default because it's almost always what you want. If one of the dishes for a course is ruined, the course is off, so finishing the other two is wasted work. Sometimes you do want siblings to survive each other's failures. Picture a reminder sent by text, by email and by phone, where any one of them is enough. Then you ask for it with a supervisor, the subject of lesson 6 of this track.

The picture breaks on timing. A real cook pulls the pans off the heat at once. A coroutine hears the cancel only at its next suspension point, so a child busy with a long calculation or a blocking call finishes that first. Lesson 5 of this track shows how to cooperate.

So a failure can't escape the tree. The trouble starts when the work was never in the tree at all.

sections.h: GlobalScope cuts work loose from the tree
sections.body:
`GlobalScope` is a scope with no job. A coroutine launched in it has no parent, so none of the rules above apply. Nothing waits for it, nothing cancels it, and its exception goes to the thread's uncaught exception handler, the code that runs when an exception escapes a thread. That usually means a log line nobody reads.

```kotlin
suspend fun startStock(pot: String) {
    GlobalScope.launch { simmerStock(pot) }   // returns at once; the stock is an orphan
}
```

```java
// Java equivalent: a task on a shared, app-wide pool; nothing ties it to the dinner
void startStock(String pot) {
    SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> simmerStock(pot));   // returns at once; the stock is an orphan
}
```

The caller of `startStock` thinks the stock is part of its dinner. It isn't. When the guests call the dinner off and the dinner coroutine is cancelled, the stock keeps simmering. `LeakedWork`, in the Try it below, cancels the dinner at 250 ms. Predict how many more steps the stock prints:

```text
  [123 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 0
  [234 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 1
[266 ms] dinner cancelled (the guests called it off)
  [335 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 2
  [436 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 3
  [537 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 4
  [637 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 5
[769 ms] main done
```

Four more steps, in a house where dinner was called off. This is a **leaked coroutine**: work that outlives everything that knows about it. In a test, it keeps running after the test has finished and may break the next one. When the program shuts down, it can still be writing to a file that's being closed. With `coroutineScope { launch { } }` instead, the stock is a child of the dinner, and nothing prints after the cancel but `main done`.

kotlinx.coroutines marks `GlobalScope` with `@DelicateCoroutinesApi`, so you have to opt in, that is, add an annotation that says you know what you're doing. Its docs still call using it an antipattern, a habit that looks helpful and causes trouble. They also warn about the obvious workaround. `CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { }` inside a function creates a brand-new root scope on every call and has every one of the same problems. It just doesn't ask you to opt in.

The fix depends on what you meant. If the caller should wait for the work, call it directly, or use `coroutineScope { launch { } }` when it runs alongside other work. If the work really should outlive the call, something with a longer life has to own it: an object with a scope of its own, which the next section builds. And if the work must survive the program stopping, a coroutine is the wrong home for it. Write it down somewhere that lasts, such as a file or a database, and let a background worker pick it up from there.

There's one fair use of `GlobalScope`: a coroutine that lives exactly as long as the whole program, such as one started in `main` that reports statistics until the program ends.

**A coroutine with no parent has no owner. Give every coroutine a scope that waits for it.**

So who should own work that outlives a single call?

sections.h: A class that runs background work owns a scope and closes it

compare.title: Work that can't leak: StructuredTaskScope vs coroutineScope

java.title: MainCourse.java (preview in JDK 25, JEP 505: compile and run with --enable-preview)

kotlin.title: MainCourse.kt

compare.note: The idea is the same in both: subtasks can't outlive the block that started them, the first failure cancels the siblings, and the caller gets one exception. In Java each subtask is a virtual thread running blocking code, and cancelling means interrupting it. In Kotlin each child is a coroutine, and a cancel reaches it at its next suspension point. The bigger practical difference is maturity. In JDK 25, `StructuredTaskScope` is a preview API, one the JDK ships for trying out and may still change, and it needs `--enable-preview`, and its shape has changed between previews (the JDK 21 to 24 previews used a different API, based on subclasses). In Kotlin, every `launch` and `async` already joins the tree, including calls deep inside other suspend functions, and you get the guarantee without asking for it.

worked.title: Give a pantry checker a scope it owns

steps.say: A small app checks the pantry every 30 seconds and refreshes the shopping list. It was written with `GlobalScope`. After the app has closed its database, the loop keeps calling it, and in tests one instance's loop runs on into the next test.
Give the class its own scope, created once, with the dispatcher passed in so a test can pass a test dispatcher. A `CoroutineName` makes the loop easy to spot in debug output.

Launch into that scope. Catch the failure of a single refresh inside the loop, so that one bad check doesn't end the loop, and, with a plain `Job`, cancel the whole scope. Rethrow `CancellationException` (lesson 5 of this track explains why).

Close the scope when the owner's life ends: when the app shuts down, and in `@AfterEach` in a test. `cancel()` returns at once; use `cancelAndJoin()` from suspend code when you must wait for the loop to stop.

Self-check: a friend suggests `fun start() = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { ... }` to get rid of the opt-in annotation. Why is that no better? (Each call makes a new root scope that nothing holds on to. Nobody can cancel it, so it leaks exactly like `GlobalScope`.)

lab.title: Stop the dinner from leaking work
steps: Meet the code. `cookCourse` cooks every dish of a course at once, and `Oven` bakes trays in the background until the program calls `switchOff`. Both start their work in `GlobalScope`. Run the tests: five of seven fail. Read the messages: `cookCourse` returns before any dish is done, and `switchOff` stops nothing.
Fix `cookCourse`: replace `GlobalScope` with `coroutineScope`, so every dish is a child of the call. The three `cookCourse` tests should now pass.
In `Oven`, add a private scope built from `context + Job()`, and make `put` launch into it.
Write `switchOff` so it cancels the scope's job and waits for the children to stop. Make `put` throw `IllegalStateException` once the scope is no longer active.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: `coroutineScope { for (dish in dishes) launch { cook(dish) } }` is the whole fix for `cookCourse`.
`check(scope.isActive) { "the oven is switched off" }` throws `IllegalStateException` with that message. `isActive` on a scope comes from `kotlinx.coroutines.isActive`.
`job` is an extension property on `CoroutineContext` (import `kotlinx.coroutines.job`). `cancelAndJoin()` is an extension on `Job`.
The tests pass `StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)` as the context, so your scope runs on virtual time, the test's pretend clock, and `switchOff` returns at virtual time 0.

drill.title: An owned scope from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a class `Dishwasher(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher)` with `fun wash(load: String): Job`, which washes a load in the background, and `suspend fun close()`, which cancels every load still washing and waits until they have stopped. Assume a suspend function `runCycle(load)` exists.

alt.title: Java equivalent

recap: Every `launch` and `async` makes a child of the scope's job, so concurrent work forms a tree that matches the code.
A parent completes only after all of its children complete; `coroutineScope` returns after its slowest child.

A child's failure cancels the parent and all the siblings, then comes out as one exception at the scope. A cancel only travels down, and a child that ends with `CancellationException` doesn't alarm its parent.
`GlobalScope`, or a new `CoroutineScope(...)` inside a function, makes orphans: nothing waits for them, cancels them or sees their failures.
Work that outlives a call belongs to a class that owns a scope, launches into it, and cancels it when its own life ends.
The limit: the tree stops coroutines only at suspension points, and only while the program runs. A child busy computing finishes first, and nothing in memory survives a restart.
closing:
We started with a dinner where a course goes out only when all its dishes are ready. Coroutines keep the same tree: a parent waits for its children, a failure goes up and stops the siblings, and a cancel goes down. `GlobalScope` puts a pan on outside the tree, and an owned scope gives long-lived work a home with an off switch.

Now search your own code for `GlobalScope`, and for `CoroutineScope(` inside a function body. Each hit is work that nobody waits for and nobody stops.

Next, we'll look at what else the context carries. Which thread does a coroutine run on, and how do you send one step of it somewhere else?

options: `done` prints at 1 s, then the scope throws `IOException`
The `IOException` is printed by the uncaught handler, and the scope returns normally
At about 100 ms the second child is cancelled, `done` never prints, and the scope throws `IOException`
The scope returns normally at 1 s, because `launch` swallows exceptions
quiz.why: The failed child cancels the scope's job, which cancels its sibling. The scope waits for the sibling to stop, then rethrows the original exception to its caller. Nothing waits for the full second.

quiz.q: A child coroutine ends by throwing `CancellationException`. What happens to its parent and its siblings?
options: Nothing: the child counts as cancelled, and the parent isn't told
The parent is cancelled, and so are the siblings
The parent rethrows the `CancellationException` to its caller
The siblings are cancelled, but the parent keeps running
quiz.why: A `CancellationException` means "I was cancelled", not "I failed". The child cancels its own children, but the parent keeps going. Only other exceptions travel up. Lesson 5 of this track shows why that makes swallowing it dangerous.

quiz.q: A function calls `GlobalScope.launch { copyPhotos(album) }` and returns. A minute later the program shuts down while the copy is still running. What stops the copy?
options: The caller's scope, which cancels it when the function returns
The JVM, which cancels every coroutine politely at shutdown
`runBlocking` at the top of the call stack
Nothing in coroutines: it runs until it finishes, or until the JVM exits
quiz.why: A `GlobalScope` coroutine has no parent, so no owner's end of life reaches it. It stops when it finishes, or when the JVM dies, possibly halfway through. If it must be stopped cleanly, it needs an owner with a scope that is cancelled at shutdown.

quiz.q: A kitchen timer screen in an app starts a ticking loop when it opens. Where should the loop's coroutine live?
options: In `GlobalScope`, because it outlives any single button click
In a scope owned by the screen, cancelled when the screen closes
In `runBlocking` on the screen's thread
In a new `CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO)` created inside the code that opens the screen
quiz.why: The loop lives exactly as long as the screen, so the screen should own the scope and cancel it when it closes. A new scope created in the opening code has no owner and leaks like `GlobalScope`. `runBlocking` would freeze the screen's thread.

options: 42, at once, because `launch` returns immediately
42, after about 200 ms, when the child finishes
Unit, because the last expression is `launch`
It never returns, because nobody joins the child
quiz.why: The block's value is 42, but `coroutineScope` returns only after every child has completed. You don't need `join`: waiting for children is the scope's job.

flashcards.front: When does a parent coroutine complete?
flashcards.back: Only after its own block and all of its children have completed.

flashcards.front: In a regular `coroutineScope`, one child throws an exception. What happens?
flashcards.back: The scope is cancelled, which cancels the other children. The scope waits for them to stop, then rethrows the exception to its caller.

flashcards.front: A child ends with `CancellationException`. Is its parent cancelled?
flashcards.back: No. It counts as cancelled, not failed, so the parent isn't told.

flashcards.front: Which way does cancellation travel in the job tree?
flashcards.back: Down only. Cancelling a parent cancels all of its children; cancelling a child leaves the parent alone.

flashcards.front: Why is `GlobalScope.launch` inside a function a leak?
flashcards.back: The coroutine has no parent: nothing waits for it, nothing cancels it when the caller is cancelled, and its failure goes to the uncaught exception handler.

flashcards.front: How should a class that starts background coroutines be built?
flashcards.back: Own one `CoroutineScope(context + Job())` as a field, launch into it, and cancel it (or `cancelAndJoin` it) when the owner's life ends.

terms.plain: Concurrent work forms a tree that matches the code: children can't outlive their parent, and failures and cancels follow the tree.
The job a new coroutine attaches to. It waits for its children, and cancels them when it's cancelled.
A coroutine started in a scope. Its failure cancels its parent, unless the parent is a supervisor.
A coroutine context that holds a job. New coroutines started in it become that job's children.
A scope with no job. Coroutines started there have no parent and belong to no tree.
A coroutine that keeps running after everything that cared about it has gone, like a pan left on in an empty house.

explain_back.prompt: A friend wants to start the stock with `GlobalScope.launch` inside `cookDinner()`, "so dinner returns sooner". Explain what they lose, and what you would do instead.
explain_back.answer: A coroutine in GlobalScope has no parent, so it's outside the job tree. Nothing waits for it, nothing cancels it when the dinner is cancelled or the program shuts down, and if it fails, the exception goes to the uncaught handler instead of to anyone who can react. If dinner really shouldn't wait for the stock, the stock needs a real owner: an object with its own scope, which we cancel and join when the kitchen closes. If dinner should wait, `coroutineScope { launch { ... } }` keeps it a child. And if the work must survive the program stopping, a coroutine is the wrong place for it: record it somewhere durable first, such as a database, and let a background worker with an owned scope pick it up.

deeper.body:
An owned scope doesn't have to be a separate root. `Job(parent)` creates a job that is a child of another one, so `CoroutineScope(dispatcher + Job(appJob))` gives you a scope for one part of the program that is cancelled when the application's job is cancelled. With a plain `Job`, the link also works upwards: a failure in that part cancels `appJob` too. That's usually not what you want for a long-lived part of a program, which is one reason lesson 6 of this track reaches for `SupervisorJob(parent)`.

The tree is also how kotlinx.coroutines reports problems. When several children fail, the first exception wins, and the others are attached to it as suppressed exceptions. When you print a stack trace from a failed scope, look at the suppressed list before you decide that only one thing went wrong.

The kotlinx-coroutines-debug module can print the live coroutines of a running JVM with their states and where each one was created (`DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines()`). It isn't on this lab's classpath, but it's the tool to reach for when you suspect a leak in a real program. Without it, the cheap trick from the Try it, walking `job.children` from a known root, already tells you how much work an object still has in flight. Showing a count like the lab's `inOven` on a status page is a cheap way to spot work that never finishes.
